subtopic: TOURIST SPENDING
TOURIST SPENDING
speechtext: How does the dominion bureau of statistics arrive at an estimate of tourist spending in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: TOURIST SPENDING
speechtext:
In estimating travel expenditures in Canada average expenditure rates per person or per vehicle are applied to the volume of various 50433-133
types of traffic. Average expenditure rates are obtained by sample questionnaires and figures on volume of traffic are based on a count made by Canadian customs and immigration officers of all non-residents of Canada as they enter the country. Due to the heterogeneous nature of the traffic it is necessary to sort out heavy spending categories from light spending categories and to apply suitable expenditure rates to the volume of each type of travel. Where possible, classifications already in use by Canadian customs and immigration officials are made use of and supplementary procedures are used where existing classifications do not provide a suitable breakdown of traffic. Separate records of arrivals from overseas are maintained by immigration officials according to country of last residence and type of transportation.
Customs regulations require the use of a traveller's vehicle permit for all vehicles which remain in Canada longer than 48 hours or which travel beyond the jurisdiction of the port of entry. This is the most important of all types of traffic entering Canada and is subjected to a very thorough examination. Principal items appearing on the permits are transferred to mechanical tabulation cards which enables a detailed analysis of this type of traffic. Heavy spending groups such as summer residents, commuters, and locals are sorted out and appropriate rates of expenditure applied. The remaining permits are subjected to a further breakdown by which the large number of cars which stay one day and two days are handled separately from the smaller number which stay for longer visits. Full detail is also made available for this group of longer term visitor. The source of the average expenditure rate is the question on the back of the traveller's vehicle permit asking how much was spent in Canada for all purposes, such as gas, oil, repairs, lodging, food, beverages, merchandise, amusements, etc. Although this is a voluntary question an answer is given on over 60 per cent of the permits.
The remainder of the non-resident automobiles not required to apply for travellers' vehicle permits is heavy in volume but the rate of spending is low due to the short visit and local nature of the traffic and is treated separately from the permit type. The expenditures of this group also are estimated on the basis on a substantial sample of reported expenditures.

Questions
Persons arriving by common carrier are classified by type of transportation used, namely, train, boat, through bus and plane. Sample expenditures are collected by the United States department of commerce and the average rates for each type of traffic are furnished to the dominion bureau of statistics. Appropriate adjustments are made to the records of the volume of entries by common carrier to deal with purely in-transit traffic where expenditures in Canada are negligible.
All United States travellers to Canada, not already referred to, are grouped into a residual class called "other travellers". This group consists of persons proceeding on foot or by ferry, taxi, motorcycle, bicycle or local bus. This group is also treated separately from other types of traffic as the average rate of expenditure is much lower than other types.

subtopic: T.C.A. TRIP CYCLES

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: T.C.A. TRIP CYCLES
speechtext:
1.	Has any change been made in the cycle of trips assigned to pilots flying Trans-Canada Air Lines aircraft between Montreal and Toronto on the one hand and Bermuda and Tampa, Florida,

on the other, since the crash of a Super Constellation aircraft near Brampton, Ontario, on its return from Tampa, Florida, on December 17, 1954?
2.	If so, what were the details of any such
change?
3.	On what date was any such change made?
4.	If no change in this cycle of trips has been made, is any change under consideration?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: T.C.A. TRIP CYCLES
speechtext:
On January 5 a cycle change was made due to the fact that the loss of the Super Constellation at Brampton, coupled with the continuation of six weekly trans-Atlantic and one daily transcontinental Super Constellation flights required the exclusive use of North Stars on the services to Tampa and therefore a crew routing change, due to the difference in flying speeds of the two aircraft.
On January 10 a routine cycle change was made affecting the pilots' 'reserve' day.
On January 27 a further cycle change was made as at that time the usual seasonal reduction from six to five weekly services was made in the trans-Atlantic service, and this in turn permitted the use of Super Constellations again on the Tampa services, which in turn called for the reapplication of a cycle similar to that in effect prior to January 5.
On February 20 another cycle change was instituted eliminating a week-end crew layover at Tampa.
The cycle changes associated with the temporary substitution of North Star for Super Constellation equipment are unusual. The other changes are quite normal. Crew cycles alter frequently during the year, as changes are made in timetables, flight frequency and flight routing. No consideration is being given to any over-all reduction in pilots' on-duty time or airborne time from the figures called for in the current company agreement with the Canadian air line pilots' association, the terms of which in respect to maximum hours of flying have been in force for some years.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to extend the benefits of the Municipal Grants Act and to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution appeared on the order paper last year and, for reasons which I think were well known at the time, it was not possible to proceed with it during last session. It is the same resolution substantially, and the same results will ensue that would have followed upon the passage of the legislation last year. However, some slight change has been made in it and, because this is an extremely complicated statute and permits the payment of moneys for several different reasons to municipalities, I propose to read a statement as to what the legislation will bring about.
Hon. members will recall that the Municipal Grants Act providing for grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes came into effect on June 30, 1951, and its predecessor, the municipal grants regulations, on January 1, 1950.
It will be remembered that the act provides for three kinds of grants: ordinary or annual grants in lieu of real property taxes; transitional grants which provide a measure of relief to municipalities for loss of real property tax revenue in cases where taxable property has been acquired by the federal government after December 31, 1948; and grants in lieu of special assessments for local improvements.
The grants authorized by the act are related to federal properties considered necessary for the functioning of government. Such items as parks, monuments and museums are excluded and also harbour works, canals and similar engineering works. Properties administered by crown corporations, commissions, boards or agencies established to perform special functions are also excluded since these agencies have been instructed to make arrangements directly with municipalities for payments in lieu of taxes that are fair and equitable.
The program has been in effect for five years. During that period the grant formula has given reasonable satisfaction and the payments have assisted materially those municipalities which contain an abnormal concentration of federal property within their
Municipal Grants Act boundaries. This abnormal concentration has hitherto been defined as an amount of federal property exceeding 4 per cent in value of the total value of taxable and federal property in a municipality. At present 48 municipalities are in receipt of annual grants.
It is now felt that in the light of the experience gained in the administration of the act, the scope of these grants ought to be broadened so that a larger number of municipalities may qualify for these annual grants. It is proposed to increase this number by reducing the minimum percentage factor from 4 per cent to 2 per cent. The bill will also liberalize the formula in two other ways. The first will increase the payments by relating the grant to the ratio of federal property to taxable property only, instead of the ratio of federal property to taxable and federal property combined. The second will remove the 75 per cent factor. The combined effect will be to calculate the grants at the full real property tax rate.
These are the most important changes proposed in the bill, and they relate to the annual grants paid under section 5 of the act. Another change will make it clear that ornamental features which add substantially to cost, but not to functional utility, are to be excluded from the assessment base of annual grants.
It is also proposed to exclude certain buildings and the land appurtenant thereto from the property covered by the Ottawa grant, and make instead a separate grant related to the cost to the city of servicing that property. This treatment would be more in conformity with the grants paid by the United Kingdom government on the houses of parliament in London and other buildings.
It is further proposed to exclude Indian reserves from the definition of federal property, because our experience has been that recognition of the value of municipal services can best be dealt with by the government department supervising the reserves.
No substantial changes are proposed for the second and third kinds of grant to which I have referred, which are described in section 6 and section 7 of the act. However, in one respect the scope of both these grants has been enlarged. The present act excludes from a grant properties which, after acquisition by the crown, are put to such public uses as parks, historical sites, etc., which are by definition not federal property. The bill will permit grants under section 6 and section 7 relating to properties in this category notwithstanding their exclusion from the base of annual grants under section 5.

In other words it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of one one-thousandth of our total expenditure. I want to make a few observations going back to the original statement made by the minister's predecessor in 1949, because it seems to me that it got us off on the wrong foot. These payments have been regarded as ex gratia payments. That is clear from what the then

minister of finance said on November 14, 1949, as found at page 1704 of Hansard:
* * . in any program of federal grants in lieu of municipal taxes, it would be unfair to municipalities generally to base the grants on acceptance by the central government of responsibility for a full equivalent of ordinary taxes.
That does not seem to me a self-evident proposition at all. I do not intend to labour it. I am merely going to point out that it seems to me that background affects the whole thinking about this matter and really gives the government the comfortable feeling that if they do anything at all they are doing more than they are called on to do, and they feel full of virtue for whatever is done, however small it may be. I am not going to deal with the legal right of tax exemptions for crown property which has existed and which is confirmed by the British North America Act. The case of Great Britain has been instanced, but my understanding of the relationship of the unitary state of Britain with its municipalities is that it is infinitely closer than the relationship here; that the central government there has constant regard for the position of the municipalities, and therefore that illustration is really meaningless for all practical purposes.
Another thing which seems meaningless to me is the arbitrary figure of 4 per cent, now reduced to 2 per cent. The mere fact that a municipality has more than an average amount of federal property within its area does not necessarily mean it is the most necessitous municipality at all. It may be the municipality which needs help the least. We heard the other day of a municipality in New Brunswick where the children are not able to go to school because of the poverty of the municipality. I do not know whether or not there is federal property in that area, but if there is that is certainly a case where the need is superlatively great.
It seems to me it is perfectly clear that since confederation the burden on the municipalities has grown greater, just as the complexity of life has become greater. Municipalities have to do all kinds of things they did not have to do in 1867; but even if there had been no change, even if we had had no inflation of money, even if we had had no huge increase in federal taxation, I still think there would be a case for some assistance to municipalities.
But when we review the extraordinary change that has taken place in tax revenue to my mind the argument becomes infinitely stronger. For example, in the years between 1930 and 1948 dominion taxes went up by 718 per cent, in other words more than seven times. Provincial taxes rose by 303 per cent, in other words three times. Municipal Grants Act taxes only went up by 50 per cent; in other words they were only half as much again as they were in 1930. The percentage of taxes is also illuminating. In 1930 the dominion took 38 per cent of all taxes, whereas in 1947 the figure was 67 per cent and the share of the municipalities was correspondingly lower. In 1930 they got 39 per cent and in 1948 only 12-7 per cent.
The question arises whether the representatives of the dominion will say to the municipalities that they should go ahead and increase their taxes. Is that the answer? I think the dominion authorities would be very slow to say that is the answer, because we are told that already municipal taxes are so high they are making things difficult for young home owners. The house building program has been worked out with very close regard to the burden of municipal taxation, and I think it is extremely unlikely that any serious person will argue that municipal taxes should be greatly increased.
I come now to the proposal of the government. The dominion is proposing to pay somewhere in the neighbourhood of $5 or $6 million. Real estate taxes collected by municipalities last year were some $614 million. If you take the calculation of 4 per cent as the average amount of property owned by the dominion, then of the $614 million the dominion should pay about $24 million. I give that purely as a rough and ready figure of what might be taken as a reasonable calculation from these figures.
We come to the question of crown corporations. I know it is not strictly relevant, because we are talking here about property owned by the crown; nevertheless the situation with regard to crown corporations is affected by the attitude of the government because crown corporations are also apparently made to feel that they are not in the position of ordinary taxpayers, but are told to make a reasonable deal. That is not what the ordinary taxpayer does. He would like to make a deal which seems reasonable to him but he has to pay the amount exacted. It seems to me very hard to argue that when a corporation comes into a municipality and may be competing with other people doing business in the municipality it is not to be regarded as an ordinary taxpayer but as a specially privileged taxpayer that negotiates with the municipality with the expectation-and I imagine in many cases the result-that it will get off very much easier than the ordinary taxpayer. I do not see any real argument in favour of that, yet it seems to me that we have come very near to that position.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
We all naturally welcome any move that will result in some improvement in the financial position of our municipalities. As has already been pointed out, this measure will do very little to help solve the very grave problems that are faced by municipalities from one end of Canada to the other. The fact is that today municipal finance is in a critical state. The federal government has ample fields of taxation from which it can meet its responsibilities. The provinces have a narrower field, but they too have a much better opportunity to obtain the revenue necessary to fulfil their responsibilities. But when you come to the municipalities, I do not care in which province you look, almost without exception the municipalities are having a desperate time attempting to obtain sufficient revenues to meet their very important responsibilities. The cost of municipal improvements, such as improving streets, the cost of public works services, the cost of education, are all tremendous when compared to municipal revenues.
I wish in this measure the government had removed the 2 per cent provision entirely. I believe the federal government should pay municipal taxes on all government property. It is already being done in 

the United Kingdom, and Canada should not be lagging in this respect behind a country that faces all the financial problems-the much graver financial problems-that Britain faces.
Other countries have done better in many respects. I have looked over the provisions made by the United States government, which go a long way toward assisting urban municipalities in improving their streets through grants under a highway program. The amount spent by the United States federal government by way of grants for the purpose of improving traffic facilities within urban municipalities adds up to $175 million per year. If you compare even that one thing to what we are doing under this measure, related of course to our population, you can see that what we are doing in this country does not go nearly far enough.
The reason our municipalities are having difficulty in obtaining sufficient revenues is that their taxing power is confined almost exclusively to real property. The burden of taxation on real property, particularly homes, in almost all municipalities in Canada has reached a peak or what should be a peak. If you have high property taxes in any urban area it makes the problem of some slum clearance and home improvement very difficult to solve.
I have not been able quickly to find up to date statistics of the revenue position of the municipalities and provinces as related to the federal government. I have been able to obtain information from the dominion bureau of statistics about municipal revenue for 1952. It appears that the federal government obtains $4,500 million by taxation within Canada. The 10 provinces collect in total about $1,400 million. All the municipalities, that is all the rural municipalities, hamlets, villages, towns and cities in Canada together, collect only $900 million.
According to a rough calculation the percentage of revenue that goes to the federal government is something like 67 per cent; the percentage of the tax revenue dollar that goes to the provinces is about 20 per cent. The amount that goes to the municipalities is about 13 per cent, and out of that small percentage of revenue it is impossible for the municipalities to meet their important obligations such as the improvement of roads, public works and education.
You can pick up a newspaper in almost any city or municipality, whether it be Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg, Regina, Edmonton or any other city, and one of the critical problems you find mentioned is the fact that municipalities are finding it almost impossible to collect sufficient money to give their people

adequate services. Anyone can see this situation by walking the streets of almost any city in the country. You find the federal public buildings and provincial public buildings in most instances are adequate and reasonably modern and provide efficient service. But you look at the public buildings owned by our municipalities, look at our municipal halls or our fire stations, and in the vast majority you find the buildings are inadequate.
The federal government has ample sources of revenue, and most provinces are able to get by but municipalities are being starved for revenue. They are in a weak position. The federal government is the giant at the tax revenue table, and it has gobbled up most of the tax revenue dollar. There is precious little left for the municipalities.
As to the provisions of this act, which although inadequate are a short step toward equating the revenue that is available in a somewhat fairer manner, it has been pointed out today that the amount is infinitesimal compared to the total amount of revenue. Even though it is a crumb, it is well that it be taken from the federal government and added to the municipalities. The minister is preparing his budget speech. We are all looking forward to many good things in the budget. The minister is being given advice by members of parliament, municipalities, organizations of mayors and other groups, and I suppose it is the duty of any member of parliament to offer suggestions to him.
Naturally we will all welcome any general tax relief contained in the budget, but I do suggest to the minister that when he is considering important fiscal policy changes and before he goes too far in the way of giving tax relief to large corporations for example he should consider the plight of the municipalities. I think it is far more important as a general principle to reallocate the revenues to those at the table, instead of taking the revenues off the table by reducing taxes of corporations and some other groups in the nation who, in my judgment, do not need additional income as much as do our municipalities.
I put it to the government that the critical financial position of the municipalities today is something for which this government must share some responsibility and to which the government should be giving real attention. Although this measure is a short step in the right direction, it is inadequate and will not result in the municipalities getting any reasonable amount of relief so they can carry on their most important functions.
I do not see how we can have a rapidly expanding economy that will allow Canadians 50433-134J
Municipal Grants Act living in all parts of the country to have adequate services and to provide revenues on a reasonable and fair basis for all levels of government unless the federal government takes real steps to reallocate the tax revenues of the nation. There are some provinces that, under present circumstances, may not be having too much difficulty; but there are others, the have-not provinces, that are in continual financial difficulty; and almost 100 per cent of the municipalities are having financial troubles.
I suggest that the government should bring in additional legislation that would move in the direction of reallocating some of the revenues in this country so the municipalities may be able to discharge their very important responsibilities, and so the burden on real property-I am thinking chiefly of home owners and of farm property in rural municipalities-shall not be increased.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary for me at this time to repeat what has been stressed by hon. members from this side of the house who have spoken already. However, I do wish to say a word or two about the resolution now under consideration.

We welcome every single one he has mentioned.
However, I would add my voice to those who have already stated the desperate position in which the municipalities of the country find themselves as a consequence of their very narrow tax base, and the fact that they have to depend for their revenues almost entirely upon taxation of real property. Property owners in the country are now reaching the position where they just do not know which way to turn. Many municipalities are having to levy tax rates as high as 80 mills. Let us consider that for a moment; a tax rate of 80 mills, on a fairly high assessment. This is a terrible burden to carry, when one considers the fact that over a period of 15 or 20 years a person has to pay over to a municipality in taxes an amount equal to the total value of his property. This is a very serious problem, and I suggest to the minister that he should give it careful consideration.
He is making improvements through changes in the act which will make it necessary to pay by way of grants about $6 million. That is fine; but I would suggest that

Municipal Grants Act $6 million is far from the amount the federal government would pay in taxes to the municipalities if federal government properties were all taxed on a reasonable basis of assessment. And I suggest the government of Canada will never reach the point where it can say it is being fair and just in this matter until it is paying by way of grants sufficient to equal the taxes which would be paid to the municipalities at present rates of assessment.
I believe the minister should have gone much further this year than he has gone toward that point. Mr. Chairman, I recall that back in November, 1949, this government announced that grants would be paid to municipalities, in lieu of taxes, on federal property held in those municipalities, under certain circumstances. An order in council was passed in February, 1950, and the Municipal Grants Act was passed in June, 1951, putting into statutory form the provisions of the order in council to which I have referred.
Early in 1950, when I was mayor of a municipality, I made application to the Department of Finance for our share of those grants. However, we could not qualify, even though the crown property held in our municipality comprised one-third of the area of that town.
Let me congratulate the Minister of Finance for proposing to pay grants in lieu of taxes on federal property held in excess of 2 per cent, instead of 4 per cent, of the total assessment of the property in the municipalities.


The former minister of finance is reported as follows at page 4217 of Hansard for 1951: The grants provided by this bill are of three kinds: ordinary grants in lieu of general and school taxes; grants which provide a measure of relief to municipalities for loss of revenue in cases where taxable property has been acquired by federal government and thus converted into tax-free property; and grants in lieu of special assessments for local improvements.
The minister said at that time that the general principles and policies as laid down in this bill had worked out well, and that the municipalities were quite satisfied. With that I agree. I must say that I could not hear the minister very well today, but from what he said I am sure that many more municipalities have qualified for grants and those now receiving grants will receive larger grants.
However, there are other municipalities which I think should be able to qualify for the two types of grants enumerated by the former minister of finance, but they are prevented from doing so because of crown property that is considered to be an aid to navigation. I refer now to the municipalities along the Welland ship canal which, as you know, runs from Port Colborne on lake Erie to Port Weller on lake Ontario and passes through Port Colborne, Welland, Thorold and on to Port Weller.
On previous occasions the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Cavers) and I have spoken on this matter. We have called the attention of hon. members of the house to the fact that there is a great congestion of traffic on highways crossing the canal, and that the different municipalities are put to extra expense on behalf of the people of Canada because of the Welland ship canal. A canal beside or in an international waterway like the St. Lawrence river does not present the same local problems as is the case with the Welland ship canal, which passes overland.
The Welland ship canal interferes with or cuts across some of our natural drainage courses, and it causes a serious traffic problem when the bridges are up for the passage of ships. This is a very real problem in the city of Welland, the town of Port Colborne and on the various congested highways running toward the Niagara frontier. During the navigation season I have waited in a traffic line which stretched back fully three miles from the canal while the bridge was up to permit the passage of a boat. Then before I could reach the bridge after traffic had started it was raised again for another 20 minutes to permit the passage of another boat.
In order to handle the ever-increasing traffic in the Niagara district there should be at least two or three underpasses or overpasses. A check was made about two years

ago in Welland, and it was found by actual clocking that the bridges were up nearly seven hours in one 24-hour period. The same would be true, of course, of every bridge on the canal, but the congestion is worse in the cities and towns and on through highways.
Because of the canal and the frequency with which bridges are raised during the navigation season the municipalities, and particularly the larger municipalities, must hire extra police for the control of traffic. They must provide a duplication of certain services. For instance, they must have Are fighting apparatus and personnel and stations on each side of the canal. This is particularly true of Port Colborne. They must have a sewage disposal plant on each side of the canal. In the case of Welland provision has to be made to bring sewage from one-half of the city under the canal to the sewage disposal plant with expensive installations in order to cross under the canal.
I said earlier that the canal cuts across our natural drainage channels. In the building of the canal provision was not made for a sufficient number of siphons under it. Our townships have become urbanized. One such area in Thorold township has either to lead a large proposed drain containing raw sewage into the waters of the canal above the domestic water intakes for Thorold, Merritton and St. Catharines, or take the expensive course of leading it under the canal into the Welland river beyond the natural drainage outlet.
Four successive Welland canals have been built, and they have not followed the same course throughout their full length. This is particularly so from the top of the Niagara escarpment to lake Ontario. For instance, the last canal followed a course through the main street of Port Colborne and then continued on an entirely new course from the top of the Niagara escarpment to lake Ontario. This has resulted in the department owning much more land than is necessary for the operation of the present canal and it creates many local problems.
The conditions created by the topography of the land necessarily vary from one municipality to another, but I should like to give a brief description of my own town, and some of the features which I shall outline are common to other affected municipalities. The town of Thorold has an area of close to 1,500 acres, and approximately one-third of this acreage is owned as tax-free canal property. This includes the navigable parts of the canal with its locks, weirs, storage basins, power houses, electrical control buildings, waste land, etc.
Municipal Grants Act
Like other such municipalities the town is now coursed by two separate artificial waterways which divide it into three parts. This prevents the town being compact. It must build and maintain roads and other services such as water lines and sewers across the canal property and under the canal itself at considerable expense to the town. Because the town is situated on the brow of the Niagara escarpment the canal contains three sets of twin locks and one single lock. This makes it impossible for industry to make use of this part of the canal; therefore the municipality gets no compensating revenue from industries which might locate there.
Municipal services such as police and fire protection have been provided free to the canal for the last hundred years, or perhaps more. In this section of the canal the boats are necessarily slowed down, which gives an opportunity for the granting of short leaves to members of the crews. It also permits the hiring of some new crews and the discharging of others. Many vagrants come to the area to apply for work on the boats. The administration of justice costs a great deal in this area. I have seen as many as 22 men in our jail at one time. We have to feed them and transport them back and forth to the county jail in Welland. I checked and found that in 1954 our firemen were called out for two drownings, and they fought 25 canal fires-and all this at no charge to the government.
This is quite an item in itself, especially when you consider that the canal authorities pay $450 per call to the St. Catharines fire department when called to the canal to fight a fire. It has always seemed absurd to me that in our town we should have to buy our domestic water from the canal on a unit volume basis, that we must pay rental for running our water lines under their property, and then fight their fires for nothing. That has been going on for years. I do not think it is fair under these conditions to expect a residential area inhabited mainly by small home owners, paper mill workers and pulp mill workers to maintain expensive fire fighting equipment and personnel without some assistance from the government. I would say the government makes use of our fire department probably one-third to one-quarter of the time, in respect to the number of calls and the time spent on such calls.
Instead of the municipalities receiving, as the former minister of finance said, a measure of relief for loss of revenue where taxable property has been acquired by the federal government and thus converted into tax-free property, they are put to great expense in maintaining roads and services across these properties and are expected to

The argument is often advanced that the canal gives local employment. This is true, but the city of Ottawa receives a grant and many civil servants live here. I am certain if any hon. members pass through that district at a certain time of year they will find they can easily determine when they are near the old Welland ship canal. The interested municipalities have petitioned the government in connection with the filling in and rehabilitation of the old canal and associated lands. We hope our request will receive fair consideration by the government.
I could not hear the entire statement made by the minister and I do not know if he included canal lands in his remarks, but I would appeal to him on behalf of the municipalities in the Niagara district to give us a fair break, because we have been providing these services for 100 years.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to labour this subject, and I shall speak only for a few minutes.
Since coming to the house in 1945 I have noticed that the plight of the municipalities has been coming to the fore more and more each year. I can recall many of the arguments advanced by my party concerning the


difficulties of the municipalities, which receive such a small share of the taxpayers' dollar. I recall that some years ago when we first proposed that the crown companies pay taxes a sound and reasonable argument was advanced that they should accept the same responsibility as other industries in the municipalities, and I think that argument applies to these suggested changes in the legislation. The arguments advanced in those days by the government were repeated in substance by the Minister of Finance when he introduced this legislation on November 14, 1949. At that time and for some time previous we were told that these crown companies were of great benefit to the municipalities and there was no reason why they should not pay money in lieu of taxes. The same argument is being advanced today with respect to the property of the crown.
It has been said this afternoon and on many previous occasions that Canadian municipalities are finding it difficult to implement construction projects as requested by the senior governments. I know this applies to the city of Sarnia, and I am sure it applies to many other urban and rural municipalities in this country.
Finally, after persisting in our requests, the government introduced a formula in November, 1949, whereby crown companies would make payments in lieu of taxes. This legislation was introduced simultaneously with the introduction of this legislation for payment by the government of an amount in lieu of taxes on crown property. The minister of finance of that day, Mr. Abbott, after dealing with the subject of crown property made a statement concerning crown corporations which is recorded on page 1706 of Hansard for November 14, 1949:
Finally, I wish to say a word about the position of property held by crown corporations. With respect to such property the situation is complicated, but in general the policy of the government will be to authorize its crown corporations to work out fair and equitable agreements with the municipalities in which their properties are situated.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to sincerely commend the minister and the government on the introduction of this resolution. As the minister pointed out in his speech presenting the resolution to the committee, it was originally hoped that legislation of this type might have been brought down last year. However, in spite of the inevitable delay I know the advent of the legislation will be gratefully welcomed by the citizens of Halifax, Dartmouth and the county of Halifax as well as by the Halifax
tMr. Cavers.]

Before saying anything about the probable effect of the amendments to the act, I think a word or two might be appropriate on the principle of legislation of this kind in view of what was said by the hon. member for Lambton West. In discussing with many people the question of grants in lieu of municipal taxation, I have found that there is a popular idea that the immunity of the crown from taxation is an old fashioned concept that has no practical application. Of course that is not correct. The principle of the crown's immunity from taxation is based on the very practical idea that it is not very much use to have the taxpayers of one administration contribute taxes to a government and have some other government entitled to take part of those taxes for its own purposes. It is the ultimate in indirect taxation, and the principle has been recognized by all governments at all levels that assets and expenditures of other governments are for the general public good and that the taxpayers in general are no better off by one government exacting taxes from another level of government.
However, the principle of the legislation which we have had since 1949 recognizes the fact that the concentration of federal government properties and activities in particular areas does impose upon certain municipalities particular burdens which are not generally shared throughout the country. For that reason there is a good argument in favour of the general taxpayers of Canada making some contribution to the additional municipal costs imposed upon these particular municipalities. It was for this reason that in the original legislation a floor of 4 per cent was selected to indicate what was regarded as a normal level of federal government properties in municipalities across Canada, and the principle of the non-taxability of the normal amount of federal property was preserved by the establishment of that 4 per cent floor.
That exemption is now being lowered to 2 per cent. This will not have a great effect on the situation so far as municipalities which have qualified for grants in the past are concerned, but it will broaden the base of the act and bring under the act a number of additional municipalities. The hon. member for Lambton West referred to the instructions given by the government to crown companies to work out acceptable arrangements for payment of grants in lieu of taxation to municipalities in which they hold property. He suggested it might be reasonable for the government to apply the same

principle to all government property. With respect, I suggest to the hon. member, that obviously is not the case.
Crown companies in general are engaged in activities more or less comparable to commercial and industrial activities of various kinds throughout the country, and it is normal for substantial industrial concerns to treat the question of taxation in just about the same way. We all know that municipalities work out with industrial firms agreed assessments, special rates of taxation and so on which recognize the importance of the industries to the area and other special circumstances. That is also true of crown companies, and the hon. member indicated how satisfactory the arrangement is in his own constituency in connection with the Polymer Corporation.
But to say that properties of the federal government in municipalities across the country are on the same basis as commercial or industrial activities is of course quite erroneous. Federal government properties are in the main service properties. They are post offices, customs houses, defence installations and all that sort of thing. They are nonprofit organizations, and it is very difficult to imagine how the same principle could be applied to such properties. For that reason I think the proper and effective way to deal with the problem is by the means that has been selected by the government, grants in lieu of taxation.
Under the proposed legislation I understand that the city of Halifax and the town of Dartmouth, being recipients of grants in lieu of taxation, can hope for increases in the grants to the extent of approximately double the amounts they are now receiving. There will be individual differences and the increases in some cases may not be quite that large, but that is the general pattern.
These increases will be very well accepted indeed. I remember that before this legislation was first introduced my then colleague from Halifax and I were two of the members who, with others, were urging upon the government that some step of this kind should be taken. We were very pleased when it was taken and the measure introduced. I remember suggesting then that this was a very excellent beginning, and that the house and the country could expect the government to build upon this very good beginning. I remember there was a more pessimistic view expressed from across the house, but I am very glad that in this, as in other cases, the pessimism has been shown to have been unwarranted.

The question of calculating fair and equitable grants to rural municipalities in order to compensate them for the presence of federal government installations in rural areas is very difficult indeed. I urge upon the minister and the government that in future some consideration be given to the possibility of working out a more realistic and more favourable method of computing the grants that may be paid.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with two aspects of this question which have not been dealt with by hon. members who have spoken thus far. The first is the feasibility of constructing grade separations during the wintertime, when seasonal unemployment reaches its peak; and the second is the need for the elimination of grade crossings as a civil defence measure.
I shall deal first with the question of wintertime construction, and I should like to quote the opinions of two men who I think are the best qualified in the country to express an opinion as to whether or not wintertime construction of grade separations is practical and desirable. First, I should like to quote what Mr. Raymond Brunet, president of the Canadian Construction Association, had to say in this regard when speaking at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, on September 11 last:
Techniques permitting construction during cold or inclement weather have been known for many years and the extension of the "building season" has been very marked in recent times. However, because of habit, pressure of work in design offices and the widespread feeling that winter construction work on all types of projects is excessively costly, most construction contracts are awarded during the summer months.
Winter work is often not as expensive as is commonly believed. It should be remembered that the higher costs only apply to the portion of the project in question and not to the entire job. Then again, contractors frequently quote lower prices during the slack time of the off-season than during the months of peak activity. Better supervision and planning is often possible and material and labour supplies are more plentiful. Wintertime construction work will lead to earlier completion dates and this fact often more than compensates the owner for any additional construction costs involved.
The second opinion which I should like to quote in connection with this matter is that of Mr. John N. Flood, immediate past president of the Canadian Construction Association. In a letter written to me on March 8 in reply to an inquiry I had made as to the practicability and desirability of doing this work during the winter, he had this to say:
As a construction man and as a member of the management committee of the Canadian Construction Association I can advise you that it is definitely quite practical to do this kind of construction in the winter time.
I can tell you further that it has been the consistent policy of the Canadian Construction Association and the subject of numerous briefs to the appropriate federal authorities that this type of work should be so arranged and scheduled that as much as possible should be done in the winter time in order to reduce the peak of unemployment. Modern techniques in the construction industry have made the execution of this type of work quite practical in cold weather, except under very extreme conditions which apply for only a small part of the time.

Railway Act
While the actual cost of any project may be stepped up slightly because of winter time operation, yet the overall cost is lessened when we take into consideration the giving of employment, and the relief of unemployment, the cost of which latter is borne by the Canadian tax payer, which includes the construction industry.
It is safe to conclude that the carrying out of projects of this nature during the cold weather is definitely an economic procedure in the light of the serious sag in the construction industry employment curve resulting from our winter weather. The construction industry has done a very great deal to ameliorate these conditions and the prosecution of work of this nature as suggested in the winter months would be a further help.
Those are the opinions of two men who are particularly able to express a worth while opinion on this matter, and they indicate clearly that this work is not only practicable but desirable during the winter months. I urge upon the government that when they are arranging for work of this kind to be carried out, they stipulate in the contract that the work should be started in the early part of November, when our seasonal unemployment begins to rise, and that the work be carried out during the winter months so that it would help to alleviate serious unemployment such as we are experiencing today.
Next I should like to deal with the elimination of grade crossings as a civil defence measure, in order to prevent the blocking of evacuation routes when air raid warnings are given. I think we must remember that if an air raid warning should come in the future, it will not be for a conventional type of bombing attack such as that to which many of us became accustomed during the war; it will be a warning of an atomic or hydrogen bomb attack. A great deal of information has been given out about the explosive effects of these bombs, and I do not think there is any doubt that a warning of this kind would be accompanied by a certain amount of panic.
Under conditions of that kind, I think it is clear that evacuation routes should be kept open so that there will not be any chance of even temporary blocking. We all know that when people are inclined to be panicky, even a slight hindrance or blocking will increase their panic manyfold, and the results could be catastrophic.
I think most hon. members of the house, particularly those who live in large centres, are familiar with grade crossings in their areas where great confusion would result if they were blocked, even for a short time during evacuation. According to the report of the board of transport commissioners on the railway-highway crossing problem, dated May 10, 1954, there is no major city in Canada for which less than five additional grade separations are recommended. These

recommendations range all the way from five to 38 in the case of my own city.
The other night the minister said that he would like to know of cases where grade separations should be carried out. I am glad to let him have a brief prepared a short time ago by the city of Toronto giving detailed information of work which is urgently needed there. There are two crossings in my riding with which I am quite familiar, where the Canadian National railway crosses Pape avenue and Logan avenue. I can speak from personal experience when I say that these are dangerous crossings. There is a great deal of congestion, even at normal times of the day, and this is particularly so during rush hours. I hate to think of what would happen if a train were blocking these crossings when it was necessary to evacuate the area because of an apprehended bombing.
There are also many instances where underpasses are too narrow to handle heavy traffic, such as would develop during an evacuation. One example that stands out quite clearly in my mind was pointed out to me last summer by residents of Halifax. This is an underpass beneath the Canadian National Railways line on the road out of Halifax to Bedford. This road constitutes one of the few exits from Halifax. I do not think there is any doubt in anyone's mind that if we should become involved in a war Halifax would be one of the main target areas, and it would be necessary to evacuate the population in case of an apprehended air attack. The congestion at this underpass, even during normal rush hours is considerable. If it were ever necessary to evacuate the city of Halifax, a vast amount of congestion would occur at this particular underpass and there would be a tremendous loss of life. I mention that just as one example. There are many others which could be mentioned, but time does not permit. I did want to draw that particular matter to the minister's attention, however.
I think the time has come when we in this country must take a serious view of civil defence. I feel we have failed to do so thus far. The elimination of grade crossings is a most important part of civil defence preparation. I think we are given two choices. First, we can treat civil defence as a serious matter, or second, we can continue in the present government's attitude, and treat civil defence as something which can be ignored or brushed off lightly. The government has not, to my knowledge, proposed any plan of action, nor has it indicated that it takes a serious view in the matter of civil defence.

I am speaking of the elimination of grade crossings as an important part of civil defence. In fact, I cannot think of anything which is a more important part of civil defence. One of the important elements of civil defence is clearing an area within a short space of time when a bombing attack is threatened. We all know the widespread effects of hydrogen and atomic bombs when dropped on a congested area. I do not believe the government has given any thought whatsoever to the problem of clearing routes to enable evacuation to take place. I do not think there is any indication that the government has considered the tremendous loss of life and the confusion that would occur if panicky traffic travelling along an evacuation route were suddenly held up because of a freight train. If there should be even a temporary halt, the panic would be unbelievable. When people get panicky in large groups, a great loss of life could occur, especially if some of them were in control of motor vehicles. For that reason I am trying to drive home the need for consideration being given to this particular aspect of civil defence. It is not my intention to use this discussion as a springboard from which I can make a civil defence speech. I am speaking of this as a most important aspect of civil defence and one which has not been dealt with, and I am trying to impress the government with it.
As I say, I do not think there has been any indication that the government has given leadership in this matter, nor do I think there is any reason for believing the government will not continue to treat civil defence as a matter of no particular consequence. As far as I can see, there is no indication that the government will look at this matter differently until perhaps we have had a bombing attack, or until one is threatened. At that time, the government will scramble to do something about it, but it will be too late then.
I think this government is acting on the assumption that this sort of thing simply cannot happen here. Mr. Chairman, it can happen here! It has become very evident that the enemy has bombers which can travel at tremendous speeds and drop bomb loads from great heights with great accuracy. To continue to act on the assumption that this could not happen here is the ultimate of foolishness, in my estimation.
Railway Act
I think when the people learn too late that this government has condoned unpreparedness in this matter, they are going to be shocked and outraged, but at that time it will be too late to prevent the loss of life brought about by this policy of unpreparedness. I believe the government's shocking attitude of unconcern in the matter of civil defence, when one considers the tremendous loss of life which can occur as the result of it, is nothing less than scandalous. We have all been greatly impressed by the almost unbelievable damaging power of the hydrogen bomb. When one thinks of what could occur as a result of panic caused by the blocking of an escape route, one realizes that civil defence is a matter which should demand our concern.
I therefore urge the government to enlarge its present program in respect to grade crossing elimination for three reasons:
First, because of the great number of lives that could be saved if a large proportion of our grade crossings were eliminated and grade separations were substituted.
Second, it will provide employment during winter months, when unemployment in this country reaches its height.
Third, because it is a vitally important civil defence measure, as I have attempted to point out to the government.

In this debate, some of my colleagues have called the attention of the house to conditions prevailing in various parts of the country, and I should feel remiss in my duty if I did not avail myself of the same opportunity to make a few comments on the increasingly serious problem of level crossings in the municipality of Ste. Anne de Beaupre, in the Quebec area.
Of course, the presence of level crossings in many communities can hardly be avoided, and the resulting difficulties being felt at this time are in many cases a consequence of the economic and industrial development of cities and towns, or again to the ever-growing use of the motor car in this day and age.
Level crossings in Ste. Anne de Beaupre were no trouble at all some 25 years ago; but as this municipality now receives over a million visitors every year, the prob-

All of us are concerned about this question of level crossings, and for several reasons: first, because the problem is national in scope, for each year many people are victims of level crossing accidents and, secondly, because level crossings are a cause of congestion in larger communities.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on this resolution with regard to the report of the board of transport commissioners on the railway crossing problem in Canada. Many of the previous speakers have indicated that this is a problem not only for the federal government but for all governments at all levels, municipal, provincial and federal. It is also a problem for all our highway safety organizations and, as the report indicates, as the number of automobiles has increased and their power and speed has become greater so has increased the incidence of death and disaster at railway crossings. The report indicates that to implement and put into force all the grade separation projects and all the mechanical devices necessary to protect the travelling public would cost an astronomical amount of money and take many years.

I realize that with the increase in the grade crossing fund many projects which have been impossible up to now will be carried out in districts and under circumstances where they are most necessary, but I feel, as the report indicates, that any measures that we might be able to take now to prevent accidents and death on our highways should be taken. I also feel that, as it is a problem that cannot be overcome in a physical way for years to come, everything possible should be done by educational programs and by corrective laws to reduce the effects of this hazardous situation. The report of the board of transport commissioners on this problem contains at page 44 various suggestions which were received by the board and which appear to have the greatest merit and warrant further investigation. The fifth suggestion is that crossings particularly dangerous by reason of poor visibility or for other reasons should have highway stop signs. I can remember discussing this question some years ago with a man in my own home town, and one remark he made stands out clearly in my mind. He said that the only sure way not to have an accident at a railway crossing is to have it firmly implanted in one's mind that it is always train time at a railway crossing.
In my opinion, with the speed at which cars travel today and the rapidity with which they approach level crossings, even present provincial laws, which set the speed at 20 miles an hour, are quite inadequate. I should like to read an editorial from the Drayton Advocate of Thursday, January 27, which to my mind indicates a measure that might be taken by the railways and provincial governments to help to alleviate this situation. It reads as follows:
Dr. Everon Flath. Toronto, a former Drayton physician, recently submitted the following pertinent letter to the Globe and Mail, who published it last Wednesday. It is of much interest and reads as follows:
"Almost every day we read reports of one or more automobiles being run down at unprotected level railway crossings. In Canada there are 32,553 crossings, with only 3,230 protected. In 1951 there were 463 accidents at these crossings, resulting in 191 deaths and 522 persons injured; not to mention the tremendous property loss.
In 1952, one out of every two persons killed in railway accidents died at highway crossings. One hundred and thirty-three out of 185 deaths occurred where these crossings were unprotected. At the end of 1952, 71-1 per cent of urban and 93-5 per cent of rural crossings had no protection, except for the familiar 'cross-arms' that we have seen from time immemorial, and to which many people pay little heed.
In June, 1954, the board of transport commissioners recommended that parliament increase its annual vote to the treasury's grade crossing fund from SI million to $5 million. Even this large amount will not be nearly sufficient to afford adequate protection at these death dealing places.
Railway Act
The cost of overpasses or underpasses for all crossings would be prohibitive, and it would take many years to instal them.
But there is a much less expensive and, I believe, a very practical and effective way of protecting our people from this hazard. I would suggest the installation of 'stop' signs on both sides of every crossing, making it obligatory for every motor vehicle to come to a complete stop before crossing the railway track, under penalty of an adequate fine for non-observance. This is not asking the impossible, for, even now, all buses and all Bell Telephone vehicles adhere rigidly to this rule.
In every town and city motorists are required to stop where signs command-this for their own safety and for the safety of others. Then why should they not take just a few moments to hesitate at these danger spots to ensure their own security? I would hope that my suggestion may appeal to both highway and railroad authorities, and that some action may soon be taken to reduce this unnecessary sacrifice of human life."
Such a step was advocated by many hon. members in 1950 when the fund was increased from $500,000 to $1 million, and was advocated by the hon. member for Halton and the hon. member for Wentworth in the house the other night. Therefore I suggest that consideration be given on the part of the railways to the erection of stop signs at all railway crossings not protected by mechanical devices and that laws should be passed making possible the imposition of an adequate fine as a penalty for non-observance and ignoring of such stop signs. I realize that this is entering the controversial field of dominion-provincial relations, but surely if there is any merit whatever in the suggestion these differences can be overcome when the lives of so many of our citizens are at stake.

Mr. Chairman, many other members have spoken in support of this measure and I wish to join them in supporting the changes to be made in the railway grade crossing fund. I also wish to add a suggestion or two to those already made. The matter of solving the level crossing problem is not as simple as one might think. It involves finance and how to divide the costs, as well as the most economical way to spend the available money. We know that the only sure and safe protection to prevent accidents is by overhead bridges or subways. This means a grade separation which eliminates the crossing and therefore prevents accidents and loss of life.
In my constituency of Elgin there are six railroads. This means that we have a very large number of grade crossings on all types of roads, provincial highways, county roads and township roads, and a large number of crossings in the city of St. Thomas. Very few crossings at the present time have grade separations. With a population of 20,000 in the city of St. Thomas we have roughly 30 grade crossings, and at the present time only

Railway Act
three have grade separations. I have knowledge of one application which has been made to the board of transport commissioners for a grade separation. I think we will all agree that $5 million a year is only a drop in the bucket as far as providing sufficient funds for this program is concerned. We should also keep in mind that plans and specifications are not prepared and put into operation overnight.
The crossing to which I have made reference is the St. George street C.N.R. crossing, with which I am very familiar as it is near my home and I have crossed it many thousands of times. It is not my intention to put before the committee all the problems of my own constituency, but I do wish to bring to their attention some of the difficulties involved in reaching a solution to the problem before grade separations could be commenced. The elimination of this particular crossing has been talked about for at least 25 years, and is now in the second year of the planning stage. There are still many problems to iron out before construction can be started.
The problem presented by this crossing involves six organizations or municipalities, namely the Canadian National, the city of St. Thomas, the county of Elgin, the suburban roads commission, the board of transport commissioners and the province of Ontario. Many surveys have to be made, and the cost of each estimated and presented to those responsible for making the decision as to what type of grade separation is required.
There are other crossings that I wish to mention, one of which is the crossing west of Rodney. Today this county road follows the north side of both the New York Central's double track and the Chesapeake and Ohio single track, crossing these tracks one and a half miles west of the village and then recrossing the same track one and a quarter miles farther on. Endeavours have been made for years to have this road rerouted to eliminate one of the crossings.
I note that there is a provision in the act which states that the board should be empowered to make contributions towards the cost of highway projects which involve the construction of grade separation and the closing of an existing crossing or the diversion from the existing crossing of nearly all the highway traffic using it. I hope that when enacted this provision will lend sufficient aid to enable the improvement of this important artery of traffic in this part of Elgin county. I doubt if there is any Canadian line over which trains travel quite as fast as the United States lines do over this part of the road. In talking with engineers in St. Thomas I have been told that this portion of track is

the fastest in the Canadian division of these United States companies, and I believe it goes without saying that it is the fastest in Canada.
I feel that when consideration is being given to these changes and grade separations, we should be building for the future and not just for the next 10 or 20 years. With the greater demand for speed being made on railroads, there is a possibility that trains will be going much faster in the years ahead. Dieselization has increased the speed of freight trains from between 40 and 45 miles an hour to between 60 and 70 miles per hour. What the future holds in this regard it is hard to predict; but we can be sure that trains will not be going slower.
Many of our highways in Canada have grade separations which were built for the horse and buggy era and are far from adequate to take care of the extremely heavy highway traffic of today. Many of these separations are too low and too narrow to accommodate the large freight carriers that travel our highways today. Provincial highway No. 3 has an overhead pass over the New York Central tracks just east of St. Thomas but in order to negotiate this, traffic must make a reverse angle crossing. This creates a serious hazard to traffic, and seldom a week passes when there is not at least one serious accident on this bridge.
The bill also contains a provision that the fund should be made available to aid reconstruction and improvement of grade separations at crossings when the proposed legislation comes into force which, because of their location, design or size are inadequate for the highway traffic using them, the contribution in any case not to exceed 30 per cent of the cost of reconstruction nor the sum of $150,000. I hope that I have taken the right interpretation of this provision, and that up to $150,000 will be made available for the reconstruction of this and many similar inadequate overpasses which must be in existence from the east to the west coast.
In closing, there is one recommendation to which I would ask the Minister of Transport to give consideration. I refer to the provision which states that in any year in which there is an uncommitted balance of $2 million in the fund, the appropriation for that year should be such sum as with the uncommitted balance would amount to $7 million. It is my thought that the $5 million should be added to the fund each year, regardless of the amount of the uncommitted balance. There could be a year in which many projects would be in the preliminary stages, and therefore the amount required from the fund would be relatively small. The following year or years, these

same projects could have reached the point where they would require the full amount from the fund. I should like to see the limitation of $7 million on the fund eliminated or at least altered to a much higher figure.

In rising to take part in this debate today, Mr. Chairman, I feel it is my duty to bring before the committee certain very dangerous and disagreeable grade crossings which we have in the constituency of Leeds, which I have the honour of representing.
Railway Act
I am sure we are all very appreciative of the recommendation of the commission to increase the appropriation for the elimination of these hazardous railway crossings from $1 million to $5 million. Personally, I am of the opinion that we definitely must not be niggardly in our appropriation to eliminate, as far as possible, the danger that has taken the lives of so many of our citizens. Many of those citizens were in their early manhood and womanhood, and in the youth and vigour of life, and had it not been for their untimely death would have contributed much not only to the community in which they lived, but to the dominion as a whole. We cannot be unmindful of the fact that we should do everything reasonably possible to banish these hazards.
Dangerous railway crossings have been with us ever since the first railway was built, but in the early years we did not notice it so much as the only means of transportation was with horse-drawn vehicles. But now, with the advent of automobiles, trucks, and transports, the danger is brought more forcibly to our attention.
The crossings over a double track are far more hazardous than those over a single track railway. We read so often of people whose lives have been snuffed out at such grade crossings as these because a long passenger or freight train, travelling east or west as the case may be, had shut off the view of a train coming in the opposite direction. I could recite numerous accidents, many of them fatal, in my own county of Leeds and the adjoining county of Frontenac, which have been caused because the visions of the occupants of the car was obscured by a passing train.
In the year 1954, we had some fatal accidents in the Brockville district, and again in 1955. Just a week ago there was a fatal accident in the same district. We may read in the press concerning the different accidents across Canada, but when they happen right in our own community, they bring most forcibly to our minds that something should be done. Indeed, something must be done to stop this appalling loss of human life, or perhaps many months of suffering.
I was in hopes that the commission investigating the level grade crossings would have recommended even a greater increase of money appropriated for this purpose. However, as they recommend an increase to five times the original amount, it is a step in the right direction. We should use every device possible, such as gates, wigwags, overhead crossings, and subways, to eliminate these catastrophes.

Railway Act
I wish to draw specifically to your attention the condition which we have in Brock-ville that I mentioned in my remarks when I spoke on the speech from the throne. We have, on William street, a crossing which is extremely inconvenient as well as dangerous; a combination of highway No. 42 and No. 29 pass over the tracks at this point just a short distance before they merge with highway No. 2. All the passenger and freight trains, when they stop at Brockville station, shut off the traffic across this particularly heavily driven highway, and there are many, many trains every day that pass along this route owing to its being a double track. Not only that, but shunting engines are constantly going back and forth, making up freight trains at this particular point. I believe there are few crossings in Canada that have the amount of rail and highway traffic that there is at this place in Brockville but have either a subway or an overhead crossing.
Not only that, but two very large schools have now been built just north of the tracks, and those children should not be required much longer to walk this hazardous path, which is ever a fear to their parents from the time the children leave their homes for school until they are back home again.
I hope that this crossing will receive every consideration, and that something may be done to decrease its danger and inconvenience. I have spoken of this particular situation before in the house, and I shall continue to do so on every occasion that affords me the opportunity.
Again I say, let us do everything humanly possible to make our arteries of travel safer, not only for the people who are travelling on them today but for the rising generation.
