Mr. Chairman, I certainly do not wish to prolong the consideration of this resolution, but a few comments have been made during the course of th.e discussion to which I think I should refer before the debate is closed.
First may I say, with a certain amount of diffidence, that I think there is general misapprehension as to the role of the grade crossing fund in connection with the projects to which most hon. members have referred. The board of transport commissioners, which administers the fund, does not itself initiate the execution of these projects, but acts upon the petition of a railway company, a municipality, a province or some other interest that desires to have the project carried out. And it is the function of the board to apportion the cost of a project among the various interested parties.

Consequently if hon. members will look back at reports of the board in the past years, and particularly the report on the grade crossing problem, they will find that the contributions the board has made in the past have actually represented a little bit more than a quarter of the cost of the various projects in the reports.
I mention this merely to emphasize the fact that for every dollar placed at the disposal of the board through the grade crossing fund, approximately three dollars have to be found and paid by the railways, by municipal corporations or by the provinces. I mention this for two reasons: I do so first of all because I think it is important to realize that the money to be placed in this fund will be more than matched by other funds and, secondly, because the very fact that the board does not pay the whole cost obviously imposes some limitations on the amount which may be spent each year in carrying out these projects.
One aspect upon which most hon. members have been unanimous is the fact that this contribution, which we propose to increase from $1 million to $5 million, is inadequate. I would like to say immediately that I do not think anyone for a moment believes that merely by increasing the amount from $1 million to $5 million the problem of grade crossings thereby would be settled once and for all. I think it is not flattering to anyone to believe that the magnitude of the problem is not appreciated. But I think those who have taken the trouble to read the report of the board carefully will find that the commissioners were very much impressed by the necessity of taking account of what funds would be forthcoming from the municipalities and the provinces, and that it would not be sufficient merely to place large sums of money in the hands of the board and consider that that would solve the problem.
For example, at page 90 of the report I find these words:
It would be difficult to justify a federal contribution which was not in reasonable accordance with the availability of highway authority funds.
And this further quotation from page 91 which, I suggest, is of even greater significance, where the commissioners say:
The sum which we now propose cannot be regarded otherwise than an estimate of probable demands on the fund under the new conditions. It may well be two or three years before the most effective amount of the annual appropriation can be more definitely fixed.
In other words, until we have had some further experience with appropriations of the order of $5 million annually, it is going to be difficult for the board to say in a definitive fashion whether $5 million will be

enough, or whether it may be too much. In that connection I would like to mention in passing that the increase in the percentage of the contribution from the fund will play an important role in deciding the adequacy of this annual amount. Until the board has had some experience with these increased percentages I think it will be difficult for them to decide whether the $5 million will be enough or not.
Hon. members will perhaps recall that in the explanation I gave the other day to the committee I said that the board had referred to the possibility that all of an annual appropriation might not be spent in one year. They had recommended that if at any time the uncommitted balance was more than $2 million there should be a corresponding reduction in the annual appropriation for the following year. I hope that this condition will not come about and that the board will find it convenient because of the availability of other funds to spend each year all of the appropriation of $5 million and that it will not be found necessary to defer expenditures because others unfortunately have been unable to match the moneys available from the grade crossing fund.
I should like to refer briefly to two other points. I said the other day in my opening remarks on this resolution that we had accepted all of the recommendations contained in the report of the board save one which referred to a proposal by which the board would make contributions up to $200 toward the annual maintenance and operating costs of automatic signals. I merely want to say in explanation of the decision of the government not to accept that recommendation that it was our thought that the moneys in the fund ought to be devoted primarily and principally to the elimination of grade crossings and to the installation of protective devices rather than to the payment of maintenance costs. At the start these might represent only a relatively small amount but they might soon become quite a substantial item. Consequently, after careful consideration the government decided that it would not recommend the adoption of this recommendation of the board. Perhaps I should add that if we became convinced at some future date that this would be a useful addition to the powers of the board in respect to the fund we would be quite prepared to consider it.
Finally, there is just one further point I should like to make. Many hon. members have referred to the use of the grade crossing fund as a means of alleviating unemployment. I want to say that this resolution was not introduced with the thought that $5 million added to the grade crossing fund 50433-135i
Railway Act
would exercise a profound influence on employment in Canada. I want to say right away to the committee that this measure is not being considered as an unemployment relief project.
I can merely add, to what has been said by those who dealt with this aspect of the matter, that if at any time it was thought that further funds ought to be made available for these purposes I do not doubt that the government would be inclined to follow precedents of the past where funds have been voted for the purposes of grade crossing elimination but without the restrictions which existed as to percentages and as to limits applying to individual projects.
I have tried to deal with the various criticisms that have been voiced during the course of this debate. There is just one further thought that I should like to mention. Some hon. members spoke of the rigidity of the formula. I have since looked up the provisions of the statute and I do not think they have the inflexibility or rigidity which hon. members have mentioned. In fact I think the percentages and amounts which are contained in the board's report are to be looked upon as maxima and not as fixed percentages to apply in each case. I notice that the percentage of 40 per cent has been looked upon as a more or less constant figure, but quite frankly I do not believe that one should conclude that invariably and in all circumstances the percentages should be fixed at those I mentioned when I presented the resolution. I think we shall find that the more flexibility there is left to the board, the better will be the administration of the fund.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RADIO ANTENNAE AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES
speechtext:
I think that the purport of this resolution is clear from its text, but perhaps hon. members would find it convenient if I were to explain a little bit more fully than is done by the resolution the three changes which it is sought to effect by the bill that it is proposed to introduce if this resolution is adopted by the committee.
The first amendment deals with the control of the erection of radio antennae. Such control is needed principally because of the use of high and elaborate structures which could be hazardous to life and property unless adequately designed and properly erected. The proposed amendment would permit satisfactory regulations to be made to cope with this problem. Perhaps I should say that I am thinking principally of antennae for receiving purposes. It is also intended to provide for the appointment of inspectors for the enforcement and administration of these regulations.
Another amendment contemplates the exempting from licensing of radio devices which operate through the use of very weak radio signals such as, for example, automatic garage door operating devices. Hon. members can probably think of other examples of the same kind. Under the present provisions of the Radio Act, these devices are subject to licensing because they come within the definition of a radio station. As hon. members will well appreciate, enforcement of the act would involve inconvenience to the owner and unnecessary expenditure of public funds.
Another amendment is deemed necessary so that Canada may fulfil an international commitment regarding the prevention of unauthorized interception and use of radio

communication not intended for the general use of the public. The commitment to which 1 refer is that which this country assumed when it became a signatory of the international telecommunication convention.
The amendments it is proposed to make are the result of long and serious consideration by the officials of my department. It is believed that the suggested changes will facilitate the administration of the Radio Act and at the same time be of beneficial effect so far as the general public is concerned.

I think it is really unfortunate that we have got to have these Buck Rogers contraptions on the rooftop of every house. Television antennae in urban areas are very mediocre jobs compared with what one sees in the rural areas. There they have really got something that is out of this world, and they are a danger to life and limb. I am glad to see that the government is giving consideration to that matter.
So far as the actual inspection is concerned, I have had a great deal to do with the radio inspectors of the Department of Transport, and I do not think there is any department of the government that has more conscientious people working for it than those who go about the country as radio inspectors. It is also my opinion that the decision of the government a year or two ago to dispense with the collection of radio licences gave these men a great deal more free time, and I am convinced that because of their strategic position and the

time they now have they can look after the inspection of these structures very well.
There is one other thing I should like to see in the bill which I spoke about last year, and I am going to refer to it again now. I think that much unnecessary criticism is levelled at the Department of Transport because of reception interference. When the bill comes before the house I hope there will be something in it to remedy that serious situation. I do not think it is right that the taxpayers of Canada should be asked to pay for inspectors to run around the country in an effort to run down and remedy interference when there is nothing they can do about it. It adds nothing to their prestige in the community and it certainly adds nothing to the prestige of the Department of Transport. The frequencies of the radio stations in Prince Albert and Saskatoon are 900 and 600 kilocycles, and reception on many A.C.-D.C. receivers is completely blocked out because of interference caused by the horizontal sweep oscillator in the T.V. receivers nearby with the result that the radio inspectors of the Department of Transport are called upon to locate and rectify the interference. The citizens are concerned about the matter, and many of them are more than concerned. The men in the department cannot do anything about it for the simple reason that the companies making television receivers and other kinds of electrical apparatus do not see fit to add filters to their products to combat such interference. It can be done by the expenditure of just a few cents.
I think that the Department of Transport should ask the manufacturers to co-operate a little more. The odd manufacturer is now doing so. I imagine that most people know what radio interference is. If you buy a Remington electric shaver and it causes interference you can send it back to the company and they will refund your money. They realize that they are at fault, but I understand they are the only company that will make restitution. I think the time is long overdue for the people who make these pieces of electrical equipment to co-operate with the Department of Transport because there is nothing that the officers of the department can do to remedy the situation short of that co-operation.
I hope when the bill comes before us there will be something in it to bring about co-operation by the electrical manufacturing companies. speechtext:
As I
indicated while speaking on the resolution, one or two inconsistencies have come to light as a result of experience in the administration of the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act over the past year which call for amendments in the act.
Both of these cases occur as a result of the provisions dealing with payments for prior service. Hon. members will recall that on electing to contribute for prior service, a member has the choice of paying in a lump sum immediately or in instalments either regular or irregular or of deferring payment
2142	HOUSE OF
Members' Retiring Allowances Act until he is eventually eligible for an allowance. The lump sum calculated at the time of the election is made up of the contributions which would have been paid during that prior service had the act then been in force, together with interest from the end of each prior session to the time of election. If the lump sum is not paid immediately, then an interest penalty is charged on the amount owing from time to time.
The most important of these cases arises out of the fact that the act provides that if a withdrawal allowance is payable, any amount still owing by a member for prior service may be written off, provided that he pays the interest owing on the balance of the lump sum which he originally elected to pay for that prior service. I should perhaps recall to hon. members that the withdrawal allowance is payable when on ceasing to be a member he is ineligible for an annual allowance or on death if the contributions, excluding any interest, exceed the benefits received under the act. On the other hand our law officers say that, as the act is now drafted, if no withdrawal allowance is payable the amount owing cannot be written off.
This has led to the result that there is a claim on the estate of a former member who died after he was eligible for a pension but before the first instalments of allowance had paid off the balance owing and the benefits received exceeded the contributions, excluding interest, and so no withdrawal allowance was payable. Had he died a few months earlier when his contributions exceeded the benefits a withdrawal allowance would have been payable and-this is the anomaly-there would have been no claim on the estate.
In addition the act operates unfairly for the member who pays for his prior service before retirement compared with the member who defers his payments until he is eligible for an allowance. If neither becomes eligible for the allowance the former loses all his interest, while the latter loses only the relatively smaller amount of interest on the lump sum he originally elected to pay.
In fairness to all, the government felt that the act should be revised one way or the other. Either every member should be required to pay all the interest included in the original lump sum owing at the time of his election to pay for related prior service, or that interest should be included in all returns of contributions, and at death the unpaid balance of the lump sum should be written off.
The second alternative is in line with normal pension plan procedure where it is
[Mr. Benidickson.l

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SALARY OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a very brief statement on the record. After all, this is one of the great offices in our system of administration, and as it has come up for discussion it would be worth while to put on the record a very brief statement appearing in Jennings' book on "Parliament", where he describes the way the office originated. I shall read briefly from this book because I think it may be of interest to hon. members, and useful to have on the record.
This quotation refers to the Auditor General, whose office by the way was established in Great Britain only a very short time before it was established here. At page 320 of the Jennings book I find this:
The present system of control has been developed not by the mere accretion of formality to formality, but as the result of a long experience of abuses. From 1780 to the present day there has been a constant process of reform. Some great statesmen, Mr. Burke, Mr. Pitt, Sir Robert Peel, and Mr. Gladstone, owe their reputations primarily to their financial reforms. Others of lesser rank . . . would be forgotten if they too had not been administrative reformers. Above all, there has been a great host whose names have been almost forgotten, who have sat on committees devising means for protecting the public revenue. Honesty in public administration involves primarily financial probity, and that has been attained. The British constitution is a system of checks and balances of a kind that Burke did not contemplate. In this sense the Comptroller and Auditor-General is the guardian not of red tape but of the British constitution.
Primarily, then, he is a referee in the football sense. He sees that the rules are observed. He 50433-136J
Financial Administration Act blows his whistle when he observes an infringement. Though he sends nobody off the field, the treasury, pressed by the public accounts committee, may.
Even many of those who have studied such matters are hardly aware of the revolution in the public accounts that has taken place under the Exchequer and Audit Act, through the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General, addressed to the House of Commons.
These reports are submitted to the judgment of the public accounts committee, and every irregularity, which in former days would have been judged and buried within the walls of a department, is examined and reported on, and the financial administration of the civil departments is then subjected to public criticism. It may indeed be maintained that, if the first lord of the treasury, or a secretary of state, should order expenditure contrary to act of parliament, or to the established rules of the service, or of the department over which he presides, the fact is certain to be made known to parliament by the independent auditor in his report upon the appropriation account of the vote to which such expenditure is charged.
I put that on the record partly to remind the house that this institution is one of the many results of the wisdom of our ancestors and is one more cornerstone in our constitution. I did not want this bill to go through purely as a matter of form without trying in this way to underline its importance.

Clause agreed to.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUORUM AT MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the present time the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commissioners consist of seven members-three appointed by the city of Winnipeg, two by the city of St. Boniface, one by the municipality of East Kildonan and one by the municipality of West Kildonan. The corporation has reported that because the members have a variety of business interests it is frequently found impossible to arrange for attendance of the present quorum. In the circumstances the corporation is desirous of having their act amended to provide that the quorum shall be simply a majority. This would serve to place the corporation's attendance requirement on the same basis as for the other harbours.
This bill is required to amend the act in accordance with the request of the commissioners.

Mr. Speaker, as the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Langlois) has indicated, this bill proposes a very minor change in the Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act. Nevertheless I would not want hon. members to think that it is not an important bill or that the harbour of Winnipeg and St. Boniface is not one of the important harbours of this country. I agree with the request that has been made by the harbour commissioners of my city and district, that the quorum should be reduced, but there is a suggestion I should like to make in connection with this important piece of legislation.
As to the matter of the quorum, I think hon. members will be interested in knowing that at the present time the quorum is six out of seven members. That does seem to be a rather high quorum particularly in view of the fact that the quorum in this house is only 20 out of 265 members.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUORUM AT MEETINGS
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUORUM AT MEETINGS
speechtext:
That bill is not on the order paper at present so I am not out of order. This situation arises from the fact that when the Winnipeg and St. Boniface board of harbour commissioners was first established it consisted of five members, three from Winnipeg and two from St. Boniface. In that situation it would have been obviously unwise to make a bare majority the quorum. Under those conditions the three Winnipeg members
[Mr. Marler.l

could have constituted a quorum and done business without the presence of the representatives from St. Boniface.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUORUM AT MEETINGS
speechtext: Or vice versa.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS AMENDMENT RESPECTING QUORUM AT MEETINGS
speechtext:
Two would not have been a majority; I think the minister has a little more arithmetic to do before he can back up that statement. By a-later amendment to the act it was provided that if any of the other municipalities in the area were brought within the scope of the act, for each such municipality brought in one more member would be added to the board and the quorum would be increased by one. As a result of the application of that amendment the board was increased to seven and the quorum was increased to six. I think it will be obvious that that is a difficult situation under which to work and the request to reduce the quorum to a majority of the membership of the board, which will now be four members, is a reasonable one and I am sure the house will agree to it.
The suggestion I wish to make has to do with the form of the legislation. As hon. members know, it is not very long since we had a work known as the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. Every 25 years or so the statutes of Canada are revised and consolidated. Most hon. members and people who have to do with the statutes of this country assume that if they have the latest set of revised statutes they can throw away all the old books. As hon. members who are lawyers know, that is not the case. The fact is that laws passed by parliament previous to the last set of revised statutes are still on the books and if there are any that have not been repealed or are not spent, even though they are not consolidated they are still in effect.
That is the situation with respect to the legislation having to do with the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commissioners. If one takes the trouble to look up the appendix to the revised statutes of 1952 to find out what happened to the Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act he will find that it was not repealed and was not consolidated. So it is not included in the revised statutes of 1952.
Being a Winnipeg representative I was a little offended to think that this legislation was not revised and consolidated in 1952. I went back and discovered that the same treatment was given to the Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act in 1927. In that year when the revised statutes were produced the original act was listed as being neither repealed nor consolidated. Now here is the picture, Mr. Speaker. The revised statutes of 1952 are for all practical purposes the basic

law of Canada; but when you come to the Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act you have to look in three separate volumes of the statutes. You have to go back to the statutes of 1912, chapter 55, to find the original act. Then you have to go to the statutes of 1938, chapter 17, to find the amending act which made it possible to bring in other municipalities such as those referred to by the parliamentary assistant. And now there will be a third statute which will appear in the statutes of 1955 to complete the picture. But you have to refer to all three of these sets of statutes to get that complete picture.
I suggest that if an act is in the process of being spent or is not going to continue to be a basic act in any sense, that sort of treatment of legislation is perhaps in order. But this legislation is the constitution of the board of harbour commissioners of Winnipeg and St. Boniface and I submit it would be better to have it put together in one act. I would hope that the minister would consider the possibility of substituting for this bill an act which would repeal the act of 1912 as amended by the act of 1938 and would substitute one complete Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act so that it would appear in one place in consolidated form.
I have before me a report on the tonnage of goods in and out of the Winnipeg-St. Boniface harbour but I will not take the time of the house to read it in detail. I might say that the harbour consists of the waters of the Red and Assiniboine rivers within the areas of Winnipeg, St. Boniface and East Kildonan and West Kildonan, as indicated by my hon. friend. This report shows a considerable tonnage of fish, hay, flour and so on, as well as a large tonnage of unenumerated goods. In other words, this is not something which is purely academic. This is a harbour which is an active place in the open months of the year and I think it is only fair that the legislation underlying this board should be in one place. My suggestion is that since those who revised the statutes in 1952 did not bring the two previous acts forward in consolidated form it should be done at this time. I have no objection to the bill being passed as far as second reading is concerned but I would hope that before third reading a change would be made. In fact, I would ask that that be done and that the Minister of Transport in consultation with the Minister of Justice and the law officers of the crown might consider my point that this legislation instead of being scattered in three acts from 1912 to 1955 might be put in the form of one complete act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITHDRAWING LANDS, CREATING NEW PARK, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would give an explanation of the resolution. Just what is its purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITHDRAWING LANDS, CREATING NEW PARK, ETC.
speechtext:
The resolution is for the introduction of a bill to amend the National Parks Act respecting the use of water in parks. Until now, as the act now reads, it has been possible to set up waterworks in parks and to sell water to people who have domestic establishments adjacent to parks. It was not possible under the present wording of the act to sell such water to motels or hotels that are also adjacent to parks, and the amendment is for that purpose.
Another amendment will authorize the levying of certain taxes for hospital services. As hon. members are aware, there is a system of hospitalization, in the province of Alberta especially, which interests the people who live all the year round in Banff park and in Jasper park. They want to take advantage of this provincial law. However, the provincial law says that the contribution in lieu of taxes or the levy under their hospital scheme will be made by the municipal authorities. There are no municipal authorities in either Banff park or Jasper park. Hence the provincial laws are going to be amended to say that in the parks the contributions can be levied from the population by the parks superintendents or persons authorized by the park authorities. Our bill is to authorize the government, through the park superintendent, to receive these contributions paid by people for these hospital schemes which would be established. They could be so established only after a referendum has been taken, according to the provincial acts, in the parks or in the townsites, I am not sure which at this time. It will be easier to follow when I have the bill.
There is a further amendment to provide for withdrawal of certain lands from Water-ton Lakes national park. A few years ago, when the chief mountain road was built in the Waterton Lakes park, this road had to go over part of the Indian reserve. The right of way was expropriated and the Indian band was never compensated for that right of way. The Indian band has had a meeting and is ready to accept, as compensation for that land, a certain piece of land which is north of that road and which we are ready to give to them. When the natural resources including lands and forests were transferred to the western provinces in 1930, it was part of the transfer that if any parcel of land which had

been kept by the federal government at the time of the transfer for parks land would become not necessary any more as parks land, it would revert to the crown in the right of the province. Hence it is impossible for the federal government at this time to give it back to the Indians in compensation for the right of way. It will therefore revert to the province, but we have an understanding with the province that the province will turn it back to the federal government so that we can give it in compensation to the Indian band. This amendment is for that purpose.
The last amendment is for the creation of a national park in the province of Newfoundland. I believe that this subject has been discussed in the house sufficiently so that I do not need to give any more detail at this time.
